lines: Avery Brooks
+1 (555) 010-3319 | avery.brooks@example.com | example.com/in/abrooks
Date of birth: 9 Jan 1998 | Nationality: Brazilian
EDUCATION
Eastmoor University | B.S. in Statistics | Metro City, USA | Sep 2016 - May 2020
EXPERIENCE
Riverside Cinema | Box Office Attendant | Metro City, USA | Aug 2025 - Present
- Sold tickets and concessions during evening shifts and balanced the cash drawer at close.
- Trained 3 new attendants on the ticketing system and the refund policy.
Brightcart Retail | Data Analyst | Metro City, USA | Aug 2022 - Jun 2025
- Built the weekly retention dashboard for 2.4M customers that marketing used to retarget lapsed buyers, lifting 90-day repeat purchase from 22% to 27%.
- Cut the monthly revenue report from 3 days of spreadsheet work to 2 hours by moving it to scheduled SQL queries and a shared dashboard.
- Found customers with no orders by left-joining the orders table to the customers table and counting rows with a null customer name.

- Joining 40 source tables, deduplicating customer records across two loyalty systems and rebuilding the attribution logic in dbt-style SQL models, raised the share of orders tied to a campaign from 58% to 81%.
- Presented the quarterly customer review to the leadership team, and two of its three recommendations were funded in the next budget.
- Trained 20 merchandisers to answer their own questions with the self-serve dashboards, halving ad hoc data requests.
Pinecrest Insurance | Junior Analyst | Metro City, USA | Jul 2020 - Jul 2022
- Ran the checkout A/B test until significance by checking the p-value every day and stopping on the first day it fell below 0.05.
- Analyzed 18 months of call-center data; my findings moved two agents to the evening peak and cut average hold time from 9 to 5 minutes.
- Writes the team's SQL style guide and review checklist, which cut query errors found in review by half.

- Automated the monthly fraud-flag extract while also maintaining the team calendar, answering ad hoc questions from sales, updating onboarding documents and covering the help desk on Fridays, which saved the fraud team 10 hours a month.
PROJECTS
City Bike-Share Demand Study | Independent Project | Python, SQL | Jan 2025 - Present
- Modeled hourly bike-share demand for 120 stations from 2 years of public trip data, forecasting next-day demand within 12% mean absolute error.
- Cut empty-station hours from 300 to 200 a week, a 50% reduction, in a replay of last summer's rebalancing.
- Raised forecast hit rate by 15% across 120 stations, from 60% to 75%, by adding weather and event features.
Food Pantry Visit Analysis | Volunteer, Team of 3 | Excel, SQL | Mar 2023 - Aug 2023
- Mapped 14 months of pantry visits by hour and day, so the pantry moved one volunteer shift and cut the Saturday line from 50 to 20 minutes.
- Cleaned 9,000 handwritten visit logs into a single table and matched repeat visitors, giving the pantry its first count of unique households.
- Wrote a one-page guide the pantry coordinator used to update the visit table each month after the project ended.
SKILLS
Tools: SQL, Python, Excel
Methods: dashboards, forecasting, metric design, data-quality checks

items.says: The same city is repeated under every role instead of appearing in the header.
The current cinema role draws first attention away from the analytics work.
items.because: For data-analyst applications, it could go in a clearly labeled additional-experience section.

items.says: The résumé includes a date of birth.
items.because: It should be removed for privacy.

items.says: Nationality should usually be omitted unless an application requires it.
items.because: It usually does not establish job eligibility and may expose you to bias.

items.says: The cinema duties should stay brief if space is tight.
items.because: They are less relevant to analytics roles.

items.says: The attendant-training bullet is lower priority if space is needed.
items.because: Analytics evidence should take priority.

items.says: The 90-day repeat-purchase change needs a clearer measurement basis.
The dashboard’s or campaign’s contribution to the repeat-purchase increase needs clarification.
items.because: The wording may imply stronger causation than can be substantiated.

items.says: The three-day and two-hour figures need to refer to comparable reporting cycles.
The time comparison needs to include the full work involved.
The stated left-join direction would not normally find customers with no orders.
items.because: Joining from orders to customers would not identify customers absent from the orders table.

items.says: A null customer name is not a reliable check for customers with no orders.
items.because: The name itself could be missing.

items.says: The bullet focuses on a basic SQL operation rather than why the analysis mattered.
items.because: A supported outcome would better show its value.

items.says: The bullet has a grammatical issue that obscures its subject and action.
items.because: It starts with “Joining” without a clear subject and action.

items.says: It is unclear whether you used dbt or SQL models in a dbt-like style.
The description of working with 40 source tables needs confirmation.
The 58%–81% measure needs a clearer explanation.
Your personal contribution to the attribution result needs to be clearer.
The wording should not imply that the presentation alone caused the recommendations to be funded.
items.because: It is clearer to say that two recommendations were funded.

items.says: The claim that ad hoc requests were halved needs a comparable before-and-after period.
The connection between dashboard training and fewer ad hoc requests needs clarification.
Stopping the A/B test when a daily p-value first fell below 0.05 does not establish conventional significance.
items.because: Repeated checking can inflate false-positive risk without a valid sequential-testing method.

items.says: The hold-time reduction needs a defined measurement period.
The relationship between the staffing change and shorter hold times needs clarification.
items.because: The bullet should not claim more causal certainty than the evidence supports.

items.says: “Writes” uses the wrong tense for a completed role.
It is unclear whether you wrote the guide and checklist yourself or contributed to them.
The reduction in review errors needs a period or count behind it.
Unrelated duties dilute the automation contribution and its time-saving result.
items.because: The bullet bundles automation with calendar, sales, onboarding, and help-desk duties.

items.says: The 10-hours-per-month saving needs a clear attribution to the automation.
The time saving needs to have been measured consistently.
“12% mean absolute error” needs an explanation of the metric.
items.because: MAE is usually expressed in the target’s units unless normalized.

items.says: The forecast result needs a clearer validation approach.
items.because: Readers need enough detail to interpret it.

items.says: The reduction from 300 to 200 hours is about 33%, not 50%.
The empty-station reduction needs to be unmistakably labeled as simulated.
items.because: A replay is not evidence that real-world empty-station hours fell.

items.says: The replay comparison needs the same assumptions and period.
“Hit rate” needs a definition of what counts as a hit.
The change from 60% to 75% is 15 percentage points, not a 15% relative increase.
The hit-rate result may duplicate the forecast-error result.
items.because: The two bullets should report separate, useful measures rather than the same result in different terms.

items.says: “Saturday line” should be identified as wait time.
The 50-to-20-minute comparison needs a clearer measurement basis.
The timing and effect of the volunteer shift change need clarification.
items.because: The shift should be shown to follow the analysis without overstating causation.

items.says: The before-and-after periods for the Saturday wait-time result need to be comparable.
The method for matching repeat visitors could be explained if relevant.
The handling of sensitive visit information could be explained if relevant.
The monthly guide may be lower priority if space is limited.
items.because: The analysis and operational outcome are more important.

items.says: The tools section is sparse relative to the work described.
items.because: Specific platforms or tools would help if you used them and can discuss them.

items.says: “Dashboards” is listed as a method although it describes a deliverable.
The methods section should focus on concrete analytical capabilities supported by the experience.
